prize_parts.citation: For showing how collateral constraints and asset prices amplify and propagate shocks, and thereby generate credit cycles.

statement.case_for: Kiyotaki and Moore (1997) supply a tractable dynamic mechanism in which credit limits tied to asset values feed back on asset prices and investment. Small shocks therefore become large and persistent. The mechanism is general and has been extended for nearly three decades in macro-finance and in the models used for policy analysis after 2008. From an economic-history perspective it also describes a recurring pattern in historical credit booms and busts, which gives the idea reach beyond one episode. The work is mature, the originating paper is a clean two-author contribution, and the credit does not need to be divided across a large team. Of the shortlisted entries, I find this one has the best combination of conceptual depth, durability and clarity of attribution.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with the 2022 prize to Bernanke, Diamond and Dybvig, which already recognised banking and financial-crisis research. A committee could reasonably read B011 as adjacent ground, even though the collateral-price feedback is a distinct mechanism. A second reservation is that the empirical identification of the collateral channel is indirect, and the contribution is mainly theoretical. Narrowing to two names also leaves out the quantitative financial-accelerator and intermediation work of Gertler and Gilchrist, which carried the idea into policy models. My assessment draws on general knowledge and I have not independently verified any source.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B011 first but limits the award to Kiyotaki and Moore as originators of the collateral-price feedback. He treats Gertler and Gilchrist as the adjacent financial-accelerator line, which the 2022 recognition of Bernanke partly covered.
responses.response: This persuades me to revise my opening proposal. I originally added Gertler as the strongest third name. His marginal credit sits in the accelerator lineage that overlaps with 2022, and he is also credited under B019, so a three-name award here would blur attribution across two entries. I now propose Kiyotaki and Moore only. I would keep Hassler's own caveat in view: where the boundary between the two lineages falls is a judgement, not a settled fact, and the citation should be worded to describe the collateral-price mechanism and not the broader accelerator.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B012 first. He argues that Persson, Tabellini and Besley created a formal and empirical framework for how constitutions, electoral rules and state capacity shape fiscal policy and development. He regards it as mature and adjacent to, but not duplicating, the 2024 institutions prize.
responses.response: I agree that B012 is mature and distinct enough to be a serious candidate, and I ranked it third. The state-capacity strand connects well to long-run development and historical evidence. I still place it below B011 for two reasons. Identification in cross-country comparisons of constitutional rules is thinner than the theory, as Teorell concedes. After 2024 the committee would also have to argue explicitly what is new, whereas the collateral-constraint mechanism rests on a single clearly credited paper. I keep B012 as an alternative, not as my preferred part.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B001 first. He argues that Mian and Sufi showed with granular data that household leverage and credit-supply expansions drive housing booms and deep recessions, and that Campbell is a weaker fit for this discovery.
responses.response: I agree on attribution: Mian and Sufi are the joint core and Campbell's household-finance work is a different literature. I weigh the case differently. The central papers are about a decade old, and the relative weight of credit supply versus other housing-boom explanations is still debated, which Boppart acknowledges. B011 provides the theoretical mechanism that evidence of this kind speaks to, and it has had longer confirmation, including through the 2008 crisis. I would not put B001 ahead of B011 now, and I do not list it as an alternative, though it could become stronger as follow-up accumulates.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B005 first. He argues that heterogeneous-firm trade theory is foundational and general, with Melitz (2003) as the core model and Helpman as a central extender, and that more than two decades of confirmation make the timing right.
responses.response: I rank B005 second and agree on maturity and on Melitz's centrality. Two reservations keep it below B011 for me. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum made closely related contributions that are not among the credited names, so priority is more contestable than Friberg's account suggests. Krugman's 2008 prize also covers the new trade theory on which this work builds. That is why I hold B005 as the first alternative and not the preferred part.

uncertainties: Whether the committee treats B011 as sufficiently distinct from the 2022 banking and financial-crisis prize, or as largely covered ground.
Where the credit boundary lies between the Kiyotaki-Moore mechanism and the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist accelerator, and whether excluding Gertler understates the policy-model lineage.
How much weight indirect empirical identification of the collateral channel should carry against the strength and durability of the theory.
Whether, if the committee wanted a second achievement, the three-person cap would allow a coherent pairing; I have not found one that does not weaken the clean attribution of B011.
My assessments rely on general knowledge and were not independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. I have no listed co-authorship or institutional tie to Kiyotaki, Moore, Gertler, Gilchrist or any other shortlisted credited name. My Lund economic-history network and my work with Lindvall and Cermeño on state capacity and railroads are field adjacencies to B012, not connections to its candidates, and I apply common criteria.
